points.minimum: States that the ETF's portfolio is owned by the fund (a legally separate entity), not by the adviser/sponsor, so the sponsor's creditors do not gain a claim on the portfolio merely because the sponsor becomes insolvent; and therefore sponsor insolvency does not by itself wipe out ETF shares. Both elements (no creditor claim on portfolio AND shares not wiped out by sponsor failure itself) are needed for full credit. Optional subdetail: citation to ICI custody materials or naming the fund as a separate registrant/trust.

Distinguishes asset separation from a guaranteed outcome: explains that the separation protects against sponsor creditors but does not guarantee value or continuity—shareholders still bear investment/market loss, and the fund may be merged or liquidated (with shareholders receiving their pro rata share of net assets rather than nothing). Must convey at least (a) no guarantee against investment loss/disruption and (b) that the likely consequence is board action (new adviser, merger, or liquidation) with shareholders receiving net asset value in liquidation. Optional subdetails: §17(f)/qualified custodian holding assets separately from the adviser's own assets; specific mention that the board may appoint a new adviser; operational frictions (trading halts, wider spreads, liquidation timing/costs); note that this analysis does not apply to ETNs or other non-'40 Act products; acknowledgment that board responses are case-specific.

central_errors: Asserting that the sponsor's/adviser's creditors acquire or can reach the ETF's portfolio assets because of the sponsor's insolvency.
Asserting that sponsor insolvency by itself wipes out, voids, or renders worthless the ETF shares, or that shareholders necessarily receive nothing.
Asserting that ETF shareholders are unsecured creditors of the sponsor/adviser or that the fund's assets are part of the sponsor's bankruptcy estate.
Asserting that asset separation guarantees shareholders against any loss or guarantees full recovery/continuity in every insolvency scenario (contradicts the question's required distinction).
Treating an ordinary '40 Act ETF as equivalent to an ETN (i.e., an unsecured debt obligation of the issuer) for this question.

scoring_rule.correct: Both required points meet their minimums with no central error: clear answer that sponsor creditors do not get the portfolio and shares are not wiped out by sponsor failure itself, plus an explicit distinction that separation is not a guarantee (investment loss possible; board may replace adviser, merge, or liquidate, with liquidation paying pro rata net assets). Hedged language reflecting medium confidence on outcomes is acceptable and should not be penalized.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, but one required point is missing or only partially met. Assign half-credit when point 1 is fully met but the guarantee distinction (point 2) is absent or covers only one of its two elements (e.g., mentions liquidation but not that losses are still possible, or vice versa); or when point 1 covers only one of its two elements (e.g., portfolio separation stated but no explicit conclusion on shares). Omission of optional subdetails (§17(f), ETN caveat, operational frictions) does not reduce credit.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error stated as the answer's conclusion, or the answer fails to state the core conclusion of point 1 at all (e.g., only discusses general ETF mechanics or market risk without addressing creditor claims/share survival).

points.minimum: Must state that in a normal liquidation the fund's assets are sold/converted and the remaining net proceeds are paid to shareholders pro rata (in proportion to shares held), and that liquidation does not by itself mean the investor loses the whole investment. Must also note that the investor normally can sell shares on the exchange before trading stops. Must convey that the final amount (and/or the payment date) is not guaranteed to equal the last NAV or market price, e.g., because of liquidation costs, market movement or premium/discount. Optional subdetails: citing the SEC/Investor.gov bulletin; spelling out the specific mechanics of the delisting date versus the payment date; noting that a fund can lose value from market moves, as distinct from the closure itself. Half credit for this point if the answer gives pro-rata proceeds and 'not a total loss' but omits either the option to sell before trading ends or the point that the amount or timing can differ.

Must address taxable-account consequences: the liquidation (or a sale before it) is a taxable event in which the investor can realize a capital gain or a capital loss relative to cost basis, and the final payout may come with or be preceded by final income/capital-gain distributions. The general principle is that liquidating distributions first recover basis and any excess is capital gain, while a loss is generally recognized once the final distribution is received. Must also say, at least briefly, that timing and the deduction of costs, taxes, expenses and liabilities vary by fund and are set out in that fund's own notice or filing, rather than presenting one universal timetable. Optional subdetails: naming the One + One ETF supplement as an example; citing IRS Publication 550 by name; noting that tax-advantaged accounts (IRA/401k) generally are not taxed at the time of distribution; mentioning wash-sale or reinvestment considerations. Half credit if gain/loss realization is covered but basis recovery/loss timing and the possibility of final distributions are both absent, or if the tax treatment is right but the answer presents a fixed fund-specific schedule as universal.

central_errors: Saying that ETF liquidation normally or automatically means investors lose their entire investment or receive nothing.
Saying investors are guaranteed to receive exactly the last NAV or last exchange price, with no deductions and no possible difference in amount.
Saying investors cannot sell their shares before the liquidation or delisting and must wait for the payout.
Saying the liquidation proceeds in a taxable account are entirely tax-free, or that the whole distribution is taxed as ordinary income, without regard to basis.
Saying that a liquidation cannot produce a capital loss, or that a loss is recognized before or regardless of the final distribution in a way that contradicts the basis-recovery principle.
Presenting one fund's liquidation timetable or cost allocation (for example, the One + One ETF schedule) as a fixed, universal rule for every '40 Act ETF liquidation.

scoring_rule.correct: Both required points meet their minimums in full (each scores 1.0) and none of the central errors are present. Omitting optional subdetails does not reduce the grade.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error is present, and the answer either meets one required point in full while partly meeting or missing the other, or partly meets (0.5) both required points. A combined score from 1.0 to 1.5 out of 2 counts as partial, as does a score of 0.5 when the content given is correct but thin. Leaving something out is treated as incomplete, not false.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error is present (it outweighs otherwise correct content), or both required points are essentially missing (combined score of 0), or the answer only says 'you get your money back' or 'you lose it' without describing pro-rata proceeds or the tax consequences.

points.minimum: Explains that a new ETF has largely fixed operating costs, so at small AUM its fee revenue may not cover them even at a reasonable fee. Framing the issue as break-even AUM against fixed or operating costs satisfies this, and so does noting that low-fee strategies need more scale. Optional subdetails: an explicit statement that small and young funds are especially exposed to closure; itemized cost categories such as legal, index licensing, marketing and distribution.

Identifies the sponsor or adviser, as the entity paying costs or waiving fees, as the bearer of break-even shortfalls. Treats the sponsor's willingness and financial ability to keep absorbing losses as a key indicator, for example through fee waivers, expense caps or subsidy commitments. Also states or clearly implies that AUM or size alone does not determine closure with certainty. Optional subdetails: the duration of waivers or caps; the sponsor's overall fund-lineup economics; the sponsor's history of closing funds.

Distinguishes seed by source and durability. It must convey that market-maker or liquidity-provider seed is temporary inventory that can be redeemed or withdrawn, and that investor seed is more lasting. Generic language like 'temporary or affiliated seed may overstate demand' does not meet this minimum on its own. Partial credit (half) is available if the answer covers seed durability or quality generically without the market-maker-versus-investor mechanism. Optional subdetails: subsidized or incentivized seed investors may leave when incentives end, which strengthens the answer but is not required if the market-maker distinction is present; the series-trust board can replace the adviser or liquidate the fund. Omitting the board alone does not downgrade the answer.

central_errors: Predicts a guaranteed closure or survival outcome, or presents a definitive closure probability, as the answer rather than indicators.
States that AUM or size alone determines closure with certainty.
Claims that market-maker seed is permanent, locked-up, or equivalent to durable end-investor demand, or that it cannot be redeemed.
Claims that fixed costs are irrelevant, or that a small fund breaks even at any reasonable fee regardless of scale.
Asserts that the sponsor's ability or willingness to subsidize losses has no bearing on closure risk.
Asserts that a series-trust board cannot liquidate the fund or replace the adviser, if the answer addresses the board at all.

scoring_rule.correct: Meets the minimum for points 1, 2 and 3 and contains no central error. Point 1 may be satisfied by clear implication through break-even and fixed-cost framing. Missing optional subdetails, such as the board role, subsidy exits or an explicit small/young statement, does not reduce the grade.
scoring_rule.partial: Contains no central error and meets at least one required minimum, but one or more required points are missing or only half-covered. The typical case is: points 1 and 2 are met, but point 3 covers only generic seed durability or affiliation without the redeemable market-maker inventory versus investor seed distinction. Score each required point as 1 if met, 0.5 if half-covered and 0 if absent. A total from 1 to 2.5 out of 3 is partial.
scoring_rule.wrong: Contains any central error, or meets no required minimum (for example, it gives generic ETF risks with no sponsor-economics or seed analysis), or scores below 1 out of 3 under the point tally.

points.minimum: States that the expense ratio is paid out of fund assets, so investors bear it indirectly through reduced fund value and returns, and are not sent a separate bill and do not pay it as a direct charge. Optional subdetails: the prospectus fee table discloses the annual expense ratio; the expense ratio is expressed as an annual percentage of assets; illustrative dollar examples.

Must convey the collection cadence: expenses accrue incrementally, typically daily, as deductions reflected in NAV. In effect the daily accrual is about 1/365 (a pro-rata fraction) of the annual rate, so the full annual rate is not charged at once or each day. Explicitly saying 'daily' or 'each day' meets this minimum in full. Vague wording such as 'gradually', 'over time' or 'spread out' without any daily or periodic accrual mechanism tied to NAV earns at most half credit on this point. Optional subdetails: an ICI citation; the arithmetic of a pro-rata example.

Distinguishes NAV accrual timing from when the fund actually pays the adviser or other providers, which follows the contract and is often monthly or quarterly. Not needed for full credit. Bonus or tie-break value only.

central_errors: Claims investors are billed separately or directly, or must pay the expense ratio out of pocket (for example from a brokerage cash balance or by selling shares) instead of it being deducted from fund assets.

Claims the full annual expense ratio is deducted each day, or that the annual expense is taken once a year as a single lump sum from the investor's holdings or NAV, presented as the collection mechanism.
Claims the expense ratio is collected as a trading commission, bid-ask spread, or a charge at purchase or sale, instead of as an ongoing fund-level deduction.
Claims the expense ratio does not affect NAV or returns.
Equates the provider payment date with the accrual mechanism in a way that contradicts the daily NAV accrual (for example, 'NAV only drops on the monthly date the adviser is paid').

scoring_rule.correct: Points 1 and 2 both fully met (indirect deduction from fund assets reducing NAV and returns, and explicit daily or periodic accrual reflected in NAV rather than a lump-sum charge), with no central error. Point 3 and the fee-table citation are optional.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, but at least one required point is only partly met. Typical cases: point 1 is met but point 2 is only implied by vague 'gradual' or 'over time' language (half credit on point 2), or point 2 is met but point 1 is incomplete. Score as the sum of point credits: each required point is worth 1, with 0.5 for half coverage. Any total below 2 counts as partial if at least 0.5 is earned.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error is stated as fact, or the answer fails to convey that the cost is deducted from fund assets indirectly (point 1 earns 0), or the answer does not address how the expense ratio is collected at all.

points.minimum: States that in an in-kind redemption the ETF delivers appreciated securities (to an authorized participant/redeeming holder) rather than selling them for cash, and that this transfer does not trigger fund-level gain recognition under RIC rules (IRC 852(b)(6) or equivalent description of nonrecognition on qualifying redemption distributions). Citation of 852(b)(6) is optional; the nonrecognition mechanism must be stated. Optional subdetails: 'shareholder-demanded' qualifier, contrast with IRC 311(b) general rule, creation/redemption via APs.

Explains that the fund can choose to deliver its lowest-basis (most appreciated) lots, purging embedded gains so that fewer gains remain to be realized and distributed later; and contrasts that a cash-dealing mutual fund meeting redemptions more often must sell securities, realizing gains that are distributed to all remaining shareholders. Half-credit if only one of (lot-selection/embedded-gain reduction) or (mutual fund forced-sale contrast) is present. Optional subdetails: tax-lot accounting specifics, effect of index rebalancing or turnover, distribution requirement for RICs.

States at least two limits, including that ETFs are not guaranteed to have zero capital gain distributions (and/or that the benefit is not an ETF-only legal exemption—any RIC, including mutual funds, can redeem in kind), and that investors still owe tax on gains when they sell their ETF shares (benefit is deferral at fund level, not elimination for the investor). Half-credit if only one limit is stated. Optional subdetails: dependence on availability of in-kind deliverable assets and AP transaction structure (cash creations/redemptions, certain markets or instruments), dividends/income still taxable, portfolio changes forcing sales, gains from cash-redeemed or custom baskets, inapplicability to tax-advantaged accounts.

central_errors: Claims ETFs are legally exempt from capital gains taxation or that a special ETF-only provision exempts them (as opposed to RIC in-kind redemption nonrecognition available to any RIC).
Claims ETFs never/cannot distribute capital gains, or that the benefit is guaranteed.
Claims the investor owes no tax (or permanently avoids capital gains tax) when selling ETF shares, i.e., presents the benefit as elimination rather than fund-level deferral.

Claims the in-kind redemption itself is a taxable sale that the fund recognizes, or attributes the advantage primarily to a mechanism other than in-kind transfers (e.g., solely lower expense ratios or exchange trading between investors) while denying the in-kind role.
Claims mutual funds are legally prohibited from redeeming in kind.

scoring_rule.correct: All three required points met at their minimums (full credit for each) with no central error. Citations and ordering not required; equivalent factual wording accepted.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, and at least the in-kind nonrecognition mechanism (point 1) or the low-basis purge/contrast (point 2) is substantially present, but one or more required points is missing or only half-met (e.g., only one limit stated, or no mutual-fund contrast). Score proportionally: each point worth 1, half-met points 0.5; total 1.5–2.5 of 3 is partial.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error is asserted, or the answer fails to identify the in-kind redemption mechanism at all (total below 1.5 of 3 with neither point 1 nor point 2 substantively present).

points.minimum: States yes, with conditions. The ETF and mutual fund classes share one pooled portfolio. ETF-class in-kind redemptions deliver appreciated or low-basis securities out of that portfolio without the fund recognizing gain (citing §852(b)(6) is optional). Because gains are realized and distributed at the portfolio level, this can reduce capital gains distributions to mutual fund class shareholders as well as ETF-class shareholders. Optional subdetails: the statute citation, lot-selection mechanics, and how distributions are allocated across classes (a simplified 'pro rata' description is acceptable).

Gives at least one mechanism limit: cash-based sales still realize gains, including sales forced by mutual fund class cash redemptions or rebalancing, so in-kind gain removal does not shelter all fund-level gains. Optional subdetails, not required unless the answer asserts the contrary: (a) securities left in the fund keep their original basis, so embedded gains are removed rather than eliminated by a basis step-up; (b) mutual fund class cash flows can impose realized gains and transaction costs on ETF-class holders, not just reduce the mutual fund class's own benefit.

States that the cross-class benefit is conditional and not guaranteed. It must tie the benefit to at least one practical factor, such as the volume and frequency of in-kind ETF redemptions, which lots are delivered, the fund's strategy or turnover, the size of mutual fund cash flows, or practical in-kind capacity. Optional subdetails: that the answer applies only to funds with share-class relief and not to every fund; that fund-level nonrecognition does not exempt redeeming investors or APs from their own gains; and an explicit mention of 'strategy' or 'capacity' when volume or lot dependence is already stated.

central_errors: Answers that ETF-class in-kind redemptions cannot benefit mutual fund class shareholders, or that any benefit is confined to the ETF class or to separate per-class portfolios.
States that the fund recognizes gain on in-kind redemptions to ETF APs, so there is no fund-level tax benefit.
States that the securities remaining in the fund receive a stepped-up basis, or that in-kind redemptions reset or eliminate the embedded gains of the remaining portfolio.
States that fund-level nonrecognition exempts redeeming shareholders or authorized participants from tax on their own gains.
States that the benefit is guaranteed, or that it eliminates capital gains distributions for the mutual fund class regardless of cash flows or cash sales.
States that cash sales or mutual fund cash redemptions do not realize gains or do not affect the shared portfolio's distributions.
States that every mutual fund or RIC can obtain this benefit, or already has ETF share-class relief, without exemptive relief.

scoring_rule.correct: Full credit (1.0). Meets the minimum for point 1 and the minimums for both points 2 and 3, and contains no central error. Omitting optional subdetails such as basis step-up, the reverse ETF-holder cost, or AP and investor taxation does not reduce the grade unless the answer asserts the contrary.
scoring_rule.partial: Half credit (0.5). Point 1 is met and there is no central error, but the answer misses the minimum for point 2 or point 3 (or both), or states the limits so vaguely that neither the cash-sale limitation nor the conditional nature of the benefit is identifiable. Imprecise but not false framing, such as a 'pro rata by NAV' simplification or a tangential Rule 18f-3 discussion, does not by itself lower a grade below correct.
scoring_rule.wrong: No credit (0). The answer contains any central error, or fails the point 1 minimum, for example by not explaining the shared-portfolio, in-kind low-basis removal mechanism, or by not concluding that the mutual fund class can benefit.

points.minimum: Answers 'no' (or equivalent: volume alone is insufficient) AND explains why via the primary-market mechanism: exchange volume reflects secondary trading in existing shares, while authorized participants can create new ETF shares (or redeem shares) in exchange for a basket of underlying securities/cash, so historical share volume does not by itself measure capacity to absorb a new order. Optional subdetails: in-kind vs cash baskets, creation unit sizes, arbitrage keeping price near NAV/iNAV, citation to ICI.

Names additional observable indicators beyond share volume, including at minimum: (a) quoted bid-ask spreads and/or displayed depth/order book size, and (b) liquidity of the underlying holdings/market, with some link that underlying liquidity affects ETF spreads/trading costs. Full credit also expects mention of AP/market-maker/intermediary activity (e.g., number of active APs or market makers). Optional subdetails: premium/discount to NAV, iNAV tracking, spread behavior over time or in stress, underlying volume/ADV, trading-hours mismatch for foreign underlyings, IDC monitoring citation, consulting a capital-markets desk. Must not promise or guarantee execution capacity; framing should acknowledge these are indicators, not guarantees.

central_errors: States that historical exchange share volume alone is sufficient to assess ETF liquidity for a new order, or that ETF liquidity is limited to/equal to its average daily share volume.
Claims ETF share supply is fixed (like a closed-end fund) or denies that APs can create/redeem shares.

Misdescribes creation/redemption so that retail/ordinary investors directly create or redeem with the fund, or that creation/redemption occurs via exchange trading rather than with the issuer against a basket.
Asserts underlying-market liquidity is irrelevant to ETF trading costs/spreads.
Guarantees or promises that any order size can be executed at or near NAV / without market impact (i.e., promises execution capacity).

scoring_rule.correct: Both required points met at their minimum, including mention of AP/market-maker activity in point 2, with no central error. Optional subdetails not needed.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, but at least one required minimum is incomplete: e.g., correct 'no' with mechanism but indicators limited to one category; or indicators listed without explaining creation/redemption; or point 2 lacks AP/market-maker activity (half credit for that point). Score as roughly 0.5 per required point, with half credit for a point partially covered; total between the extremes is partial.
scoring_rule.wrong: Commits any central error, or fails to answer that volume alone is insufficient and covers neither required point substantively.

points.minimum: States that authorized participants (or large institutional/designated dealers) can create new ETF shares by delivering a basket of underlying securities (or cash equivalent) to the issuer, and redeem ETF shares by returning them to the issuer in exchange for the basket. Both directions (creation and redemption) must be conveyed at least implicitly. Optional subdetails: in-kind vs. cash creations, creation-unit size, that only APs transact directly with the issuer.

Explains the arbitrage link: when the ETF trades at a premium to NAV/underlying value, APs profit by creating shares and selling them (adding supply, pushing price down); when at a discount, APs buy ETF shares and redeem them (removing supply, pushing price up); this profit motive keeps price near NAV. A general statement that profitable arbitrage between price and NAV via creation/redemption pulls them together suffices if direction is not mis-stated. Optional subdetails: APs often act on behalf of or alongside market makers; market-maker quoting/liquidity provision; role of iNAV/IOPV; transaction costs and bid-ask spreads limiting arbitrage.

Notes that this is an incentive-driven economic mechanism rather than a guarantee: price can deviate from NAV (premiums/discounts), especially in stressed markets, illiquid or foreign/time-zone-mismatched underlying assets, or when arbitrage is costly or constrained. Optional but valued; absence does not reduce below correct if points 1-2 are full and no claim of guaranteed equality is made.

central_errors: Claims the ETF issuer, an exchange, or a regulator directly sets, fixes, or guarantees the market price equal to NAV.
Claims market price always or necessarily equals NAV / that deviations cannot occur.
Reverses the arbitrage direction (e.g., says APs create shares when the ETF trades at a discount or redeem when at a premium) as the core explanation.

Attributes the price-NAV link primarily to something other than creation/redemption arbitrage (e.g., ordinary investor buying/selling alone, daily price resets at NAV like mutual funds, or the fund manager trading to support the price) with no mention of the creation/redemption mechanism.
States retail investors routinely create/redeem directly with the issuer as the mechanism, in place of APs/institutional participants.

scoring_rule.correct: Points 1 and 2 both met at their minimums, and no central error. Point 3 is not required, but if the answer addresses accuracy it must not assert guaranteed equality.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, and either (a) point 2's arbitrage incentive is conveyed but the creation/redemption basket mechanics of point 1 are vague or only one direction is described, or (b) creation/redemption is described but the arbitrage/profit link to price convergence is missing or only implied. Half-credit for one required point met fully and the other only partially; an answer naming arbitrage by APs in general terms without basket exchange counts as partial.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error, or neither creation/redemption nor arbitrage by APs/market participants is identified as the mechanism.

points.minimum: States that a creation increases shares outstanding because the fund issues new ETF shares to an authorized participant (AP). Wording such as 'issues', 'creates', or 'new shares' satisfies the issuance mechanism. Optional subdetails: the AP delivers a basket of securities or cash in exchange; the issuance happens in creation-unit blocks; the AP is typically motivated by arbitrage when the ETF trades at a premium.

States that a redemption decreases shares outstanding because ETF shares are returned to the fund and cancelled, retired, or destroyed. Optional subdetails: the AP is the party redeeming; the AP receives a basket of securities or cash in return; redemptions happen in creation-unit blocks; redemptions are typically arbitrage-driven when the ETF trades at a discount.

Notes that ordinary buying and selling on an exchange only transfers existing shares between investors and does not by itself change shares outstanding. Only the primary market (creations and redemptions) changes the count.

central_errors: Stating that creations decrease shares outstanding, or that redemptions increase them (reversed direction).
Stating that creations or redemptions leave shares outstanding unchanged, or that the ETF has a fixed share count like a closed-end fund.
Stating that secondary-market trades by investors directly create or destroy ETF shares, or that buying on an exchange issues new shares.
Stating that redeemed shares are resold or re-traded on the exchange rather than being removed from shares outstanding, presented as the mechanism by which redemption works.

scoring_rule.correct: Both required points 1 and 2 are present at their minimum, with the correct direction and the issuance or cancellation mechanism, and the answer contains no central error. Point 3 is not needed for full credit.
scoring_rule.partial: Half credit. Use this when exactly one of points 1 and 2 meets its minimum, or when both directions (creation increases, redemption decreases) are stated correctly but without any issuance or cancellation mechanism. The answer must also contain no central error. Omissions alone, including leaving out the AP, the basket, or point 3, never make an answer wrong.
scoring_rule.wrong: Zero credit. Use this when the answer contains any central error, or when it meets neither point 1 nor point 2, for example by giving the wrong direction or not addressing the change in shares outstanding at all.

points.minimum: States that, in ordinary dealing, an ordinary retail investor cannot redeem individual ETF shares directly with the fund (a clear 'no'), and that direct primary-market creation/redemption with the fund is done by authorized participants (APs) in creation units (large blocks), while retail investors buy and sell existing shares through brokers on an exchange or other secondary market. Minimum: (a) the answer is 'no' for retail redemption of individual shares; (b) direct fund redemption is limited to APs; (c) retail investors trade through a broker on an exchange or secondary market. Optional subdetails that are not required: the term 'creation unit' itself or typical unit sizes; in-kind versus cash baskets; AP agreements with the distributor; arbitrage keeping prices near NAV; Rule 6c-11; market makers; an investor who is or acts through an AP.

Explains the usual alternative: a retail investor exits by selling the shares through a broker in the secondary market at the market price, which can differ from NAV. This is a sale to another market participant, not a redemption by the fund. Optional: bid-ask spreads and commissions; premium or discount to NAV; that market makers or APs may later redeem creation units with the fund.

central_errors: Asserts that an ordinary retail investor can, in ordinary dealing, redeem individual ETF shares directly with the fund (for example, at NAV like a mutual fund).
Characterizes a retail sale on an exchange or through a broker as a direct redemption with or by the fund.
States that ETFs, like mutual funds, must redeem any shareholder's individual shares at NAV on demand.
States that a retail investor has no way to exit or liquidate an ETF position outside the excluded reorganization, merger, conversion or liquidation events.
Relies on the excluded reorganization, merger, conversion or liquidation scenarios as the basis for answering 'yes' to direct retail redemption.

scoring_rule.correct: Both required points meet their minimums: a clear 'no' to direct retail redemption, direct redemption identified as limited to APs (creation units), and the alternative identified as selling through a broker on the secondary market. No central error is present. Optional details are not required, and minor imprecision in them (for example, unit sizes) does not reduce the grade.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, but coverage is incomplete. Award half credit per bundled element: for example, a correct 'no' and a broker or exchange sale alternative with no mention of APs or creation units, or a description of APs and creation units without clearly stating the retail exit route. Hedged or ambiguous wording that never contradicts the correct position also counts as partial.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error is present, even if correct points also appear. Also wrong: no meaningful coverage of either required point, or an answer limited to the excluded corporate-action exceptions.

points.minimum: States that under Rule 6c-11(a)(1) an authorized participant (1) must be a member or participant of an SEC-registered clearing agency and (2) must have a written agreement with the ETF or one of its service providers that allows it to place creation/redemption orders. Both prongs are needed for full credit on this point. The answer must convey that the rule allows the ETF OR any of its service providers as the counterparty. Saying 'a written agreement with the ETF or its distributor/agent' is acceptable if it does not restrict the counterparty to the ETF alone. Optional: the verbatim definition, the citation, and naming specific service-provider types.

Contrasts the rule's permissive counterparty language with the reviewed US forms. In those forms, the distributor and the AP are the main or principal counterparties, and the trust/ETF is not a main signatory but a third-party beneficiary. Optional: that the transfer agent countersigns, and that the trust sometimes signs for specified provisions. An answer that names the distributor and AP as main parties but omits the trust's beneficiary status earns half credit on this point.

States that the reviewed forms condition eligibility on NSCC membership for orders through the clearing process and/or DTC participation for orders outside the clearing process. Mentioning both venues, linked to the correct order path, is the minimum. Specifying NSCC 'netting' membership is optional; plain 'NSCC member/participant' is accepted. The point that AP eligibility is not the same as being a market maker is optional; give it credit if present.

central_errors: Stating that Rule 6c-11 requires the written agreement to be with the ETF/trust itself only, excluding service providers.
Stating that Rule 6c-11 does not require a written agreement, or does not require clearing-agency membership or participation.

Stating that the rule itself specifically mandates NSCC membership or DTC participation as the sole qualifying clearing agency, thereby conflating the forms' requirements with the rule's general registered-clearing-agency standard.
Stating that in the reviewed forms the trust/ETF or the transfer agent is the principal counterparty in place of the distributor, or that the distributor is not a party.
Stating that the forms require both NSCC and DTC for every order, or attaching NSCC and DTC to the wrong order paths, such as DTC for clearing-process orders and NSCC for orders outside it.
Stating that an AP must be a market maker, or that AP eligibility is equivalent to or confers market-making status or obligations.
Presenting the reviewed forms' party structure as the structure the rule mandates.

scoring_rule.correct: All three required minima are met (half credit on any point is not enough), the rule-versus-forms distinction is explicit, and no central error is present. Equivalent wording is accepted. No citations or particular ordering are required.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, but one or more required minima are missing or only half met. Score each required point at 1 (met), 0.5 (half met, e.g., only one prong of point 1, distributor and AP without the trust's beneficiary role in point 2, or only one of NSCC/DTC in point 3) or 0 (absent). A total of at least 1.5 but less than 3 is partial. Point 1 must score at least 0.5 to be partial rather than wrong.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error is asserted, OR the total score is below 1.5, OR point 1 scores 0 (neither prong of the rule's definition is conveyed). Omission alone never triggers a central error. It lowers the score only through the point totals.

points.minimum: Must state both central facts: (a) AP status carries no obligation to keep creating or redeeming (activity is voluntary/discretionary), and (b) AP status by itself does not entitle the AP to a standing payment, retainer, or fee from the ETF or sponsor. Must also indicate, at least briefly, how APs actually earn (e.g., dealer APs via trading/arbitrage/spreads, agency APs by charging clients for processing). Optional subdetails: explicit dealer vs agency AP labels; IDC primer citation; noting secondary-market trading continues without AP activity.

If addressed, should characterise the fund's creation/redemption transaction fee as a cost charged to the AP (to offset fund transaction costs), not AP compensation, and may note that sponsors/advisers can waive or pay it, which subsidises the AP's cost rather than paying for AP status. Vague 'pass-through fees to cover costs' wording that does not reverse the payment direction is acceptable. Optional subdetails: payer/accounting treatment of waivers.

If included, note that sponsors often waive creation/redemption fees on custom redemptions (practitioner-vouched observation). Do not require that every waiver be described as a sponsor cash payment; payer and accounting treatment depend on the arrangement.

central_errors: Claims APs receive a standing fee, retainer, or payment from the ETF/sponsor merely for holding AP status.
Claims APs are legally or contractually obligated to keep creating or redeeming continuously, or must create/redeem on demand to maintain the ETF's price.
Describes the fund's creation/redemption transaction fee as compensation paid to the AP (reversing the fee direction).
Treats a separate market-maker/LMM quoting contract or exchange incentive as AP-status compensation from the sponsor, presented as the answer to whether APs are paid for being APs.

scoring_rule.correct: Both required elements of point 1 are present (no standing payment for AP status; no ongoing duty to create/redeem) with at least a brief account of how APs earn, and no central error. Omission of optional points 2 and 3 does not reduce the grade.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, but point 1 is incomplete: only one of the two central facts (payment or obligation) is clearly stated, or both are stated but with no indication of how APs actually earn, or with hedging/ambiguity that leaves the answer to one sub-question unclear. Treat as half credit.
scoring_rule.wrong: Contains any listed central error, or fails to answer both sub-questions (neither the payment nor the obligation fact is correctly stated).

points.minimum: Must state that in-kind creations or redemptions require positions that can actually be transferred under the relevant legal, clearing/settlement and fund/AP dealing arrangements. Must state that where the derivative positions cannot practicably be transferred, the fund deals in cash (or uses a cash component) and enters or unwinds the exposure itself. Must contrast this with transferable securities (e.g., equities or bonds) that can move in kind. Must frame the explanation as conditional on practical transferability, not as a rule for a whole asset class. Wording such as 'generally', 'often', or 'where not transferable' satisfies the conditional framing. Optional: naming examples (bilateral OTC swaps/forwards, exchange-cleared futures account constraints), novation or counterparty consent issues, other operational reasons for cash use, and the point that this concerns practicability rather than preference.

Must convey at least one fund-level consequence of cash dealing: the fund bears trading costs or market impact from establishing or unwinding exposure, or cash redemptions can cause the fund to realize gains. Must also convey that this reduces or forfeits the practical benefits of in-kind dealing. Stating it explicitly or clearly implying it by contrast is acceptable, e.g., 'in-kind redemptions avoid realizing gains'. Optional: an explicit statement that magnitude and tax result depend on the strategy, the transaction, and how derivatives are taxed; that costs may be partly passed to APs via transaction fees or the cash component; and that cash does not always generate gains. Half-credit: only costs or only the tax/gain-realization effect is addressed and the in-kind-benefit link is weak, or the consequence is mentioned only vaguely.

central_errors: Asserts that all futures, all OTC derivatives, or all derivatives are legally or technically impossible to transfer in kind, presented as a blanket asset-class prohibition rather than a conditional or practical explanation.
Asserts that derivative positions transfer to or from APs in kind just like ordinary securities, so there is no transferability reason for cash dealing.
Asserts that US law or regulation categorically requires derivatives-based ETFs to create or redeem only in cash.
Asserts that cash creations or redemptions have no trading-cost or tax consequences for the fund, or are inherently as tax-efficient as in-kind dealing.
States as an absolute rule that cash dealing always generates realized gains or taxable distributions regardless of strategy or transaction.
Reverses the mechanism, e.g., claims the AP rather than the fund establishes or unwinds the derivative exposure when the fund deals in cash.

scoring_rule.correct: Both required minima are met (point 2 may be satisfied by explicit statement or clear implication through the in-kind contrast) and no central error is present. Omitting optional subdetails does not reduce the grade. A truncated trailing sentence does not reduce the grade unless the retained text contains a central error.
scoring_rule.partial: Point 1 is fully met, point 2 is half-met or missing, and there is no central error. Also partial if point 1 states the cash/fund-implementation mechanism but omits the contrast with transferable securities or the conditional framing, while point 2 is met and no central error is present. Treat as about half credit per deficient bundled point.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error is present, or point 1's core mechanism is missing: transferability requirement leading to fund cash implementation. Omission alone in point 2 never makes the answer wrong.

points.minimum: Identifies the fund sponsor's website daily holdings/portfolio disclosure as the public starting point for daily holdings, AND explicitly distinguishes portfolio holdings from the creation/redemption (transaction) basket, i.e. the published holdings are not necessarily the basket used for creations/redemptions. Optional subdetails (not required for full credit): citing Rule 6c-11(c)(1)–(3) by paragraph; noting the rule mandates public holdings disclosure but not publication of every transaction basket; mentioning custom baskets or that baskets may differ pro rata/non-pro rata; mentioning other website disclosures (NAV, premium/discount, spread).

States that the actual PCF is distributed via NSCC's participant workflow (not a general public channel) and gives a practical request route: contact the sponsor/issuer (e.g., capital-markets or ETF desk) and/or the investor's broker (or an authorized participant/NSCC participant intermediary) to ask about access; AND does not assume a free public downloadable PCF exists for any named fund (states or clearly implies public PCF availability is not assured). Optional subdetails: reference to DTCC ETF processing timeline; noting some sponsors may voluntarily publish basket/PCF-like files; noting access may carry licensing/fees or be denied; paid third-party data vendors as an alternative.

central_errors: Asserts that a fund's published daily holdings are the same as, or are by definition, the creation/redemption basket/PCF.
Asserts that Rule 6c-11 requires ETFs to publicly publish the PCF or every creation/redemption basket.

Asserts or assumes that a specific named fund (or ETFs generally) offers a free public downloadable PCF, or that retail investors can download the PCF directly from NSCC/DTCC without participant access.

Directs the investor to an incorrect primary source for daily holdings in place of the fund website (e.g., claims daily holdings are only available via SEC Form N-PORT/N-CSR filings or only via NSCC), such that the starting-point guidance is wrong.
States the PCF is not distributed through NSCC / is unrelated to NSCC participant processing.

scoring_rule.correct: Both required points meet their minimums and no central error is present. Optional subdetails are not needed.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, but one or both required points are incomplete. Score each required point as 1 (minimum fully met), 0.5 (partial: e.g., point 1 names the fund website but omits the holdings-vs-basket distinction, or makes the distinction without naming the website starting point; point 2 mentions NSCC distribution but gives no request route, or gives a sponsor/broker route without noting NSCC/limited public availability), or 0 (absent). Total 0.5–1.5 of 2 = partial. Omission alone is never treated as a falsehood.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error is present (regardless of other content), or total score is 0 of 2 (neither point addressed even partially).

points.minimum: Must state both sides of the core distinction. (a) APs deal directly with the ETF or its issuer in the primary market, creating and redeeming shares, typically in creation units. (b) Market makers quote bids and offers, or two-sided prices, and provide liquidity in secondary or exchange trading. Equivalent wording is acceptable, such as 'APs interact with the fund to change share supply; market makers trade shares with investors on the exchange.' Optional subdetails: creation-unit size, in-kind baskets, and the arbitrage link to NAV or price alignment.

Must convey both elements below. (a) Overlap: one firm can act as both AP and market maker, but the roles remain distinct functions. (b) Link: market makers can use the creation/redemption process to offset or manage inventory, hedge, or arbitrage. Implicit wording is acceptable, such as 'hedge or arbitrage a mismatch via creation/redemption.' Optional subdetail: stating explicitly that non-AP market makers access creation/redemption through an AP. Omitting that subdetail is not penalized. An answer that implies only AP-affiliated market makers can use creation/redemption loses no credit unless it affirmatively states that non-AP market makers cannot obtain creations or redemptions. Covering only one of (a) or (b) earns half credit for this point.

Nice-to-have, not required for a broad comparison question. Credit if the answer mentions either of the following: (a) a lead or designated market maker (LMM) assigned to a particular ETF with quoting commitments such as spread or size obligations; or (b) market makers need not be APs or hold an AP agreement. Omitting the LMM concept is not a substantive gap and must not reduce the score.

central_errors: Reverses the roles, for example stating that market makers create or redeem directly with the fund in the primary market and APs provide exchange quotes, or that APs are the primary source of continuous secondary-market quotes.
States that market makers who are not APs can create or redeem directly with the fund without an AP.
States that all market makers must be APs, or that APs and market makers are always the same firm or the same role with no distinction.
States that ordinary investors buy or redeem ETF shares directly with the fund at NAV through market makers, conflating secondary trading with primary-market creation/redemption.

States that every market maker in an ETF is designated by or contractually obligated to the issuer to quote, conflating general market makers with an LMM. This counts only if affirmatively asserted as a general rule.

scoring_rule.correct: Point 1 is fully met and point 2's minimum (both overlap/distinctness and the creation/redemption inventory or hedging link) is met, with no central error. Point 3 is not needed for full credit, and omitting the LMM concept is not a deduction. Minor imprecision in optional subdetails does not reduce the score.
scoring_rule.partial: Point 1 is met but point 2 is only half covered (only overlap or only the inventory link), or point 2 is entirely missing. Also partial: both required points are present but contain a non-central inaccuracy or a materially vague role description, with no central error. Point 2 counts as half credit when only one of its two elements is present.
scoring_rule.wrong: Point 1's core primary-versus-secondary distinction is missing or garbled, or the answer affirmatively asserts any listed central error, regardless of other correct content. Omissions alone, including a missing LMM concept, never make an answer wrong.

points.minimum: States that a third-party series trust provides existing trust/governance and servicing infrastructure (board and/or officers and/or service providers/administration/compliance), so the sponsor avoids building it. It must also convey that fixed governance and servicing costs are shared or lower for the sponsor. This can be stated outright ('spread across funds') or made clear by contrasting the platform with the sponsor bearing those fixed costs alone in its own trust. Optional subdetails: an explicit 'spread across many funds' phrasing, an itemized list of officers/vendors, and platform or pass-through fee mechanics.

Must state the control trade-off concretely. Using the platform means the sponsor gives up control of the trust's governance and/or service providers: the board or trustees and the governance standards belong to or are set by the platform host, not the sponsor. Building its own trust gives more control. Generic wording such as 'own trust gives more control over branding/policies/vendors' with no indication that the platform board/host is not the sponsor's earns only half credit for this point. Optional subdetails: that the platform board can replace the adviser or liquidate the fund (strong illustration, not strictly required if third-party board control is stated), and the sponsor's role as adviser, sub-adviser or contractual partner.

Gives a conditional judgment: for a small sponsor launching one ordinary ETF with a limited fixed-cost budget and no infrastructure, a platform is a plausible or often sensible fit, weighed against the control trade-off. The answer must not present either option as universally correct, for example by noting that an own trust can suit sponsors expecting scale, multiple funds, or needing independence or unsupported features. Exact recommendation wording is not required.

central_errors: States or clearly implies that on a series-trust platform the sponsor controls or appoints the trust's board/trustees, or that the platform board cannot affect the sponsor's role as adviser or the fund's continuation.
States that building its own trust is cheaper or has lower fixed costs than a platform for a single small fund, or that a platform carries higher fixed governance/servicing burdens for the sponsor.
Claims that a platform involves no loss of sponsor control (no control trade-off).
Presents one structure as the correct answer for every sponsor, e.g., 'always use a platform' or 'always build your own trust,' with no conditionality.
Claims a new US ETF can operate with no board/registered-investment-company governance structure at all, or that the sponsor must itself form a trust to use a platform.

scoring_rule.correct: All three required points fully met (point 2 must identify that platform governance/board or providers are the host's, not the sponsor's, beyond generic 'less control') and no central error. Board-removal/liquidation and adviser/sub-adviser role details are not needed for correct.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, and at least one required point is met, but one or more required points are missing or only half-met. A common case is point 2 covered only generically (e.g., 'own trust gives more control over vendors/branding') without saying the platform host/board controls governance. Score each point as 1, 0.5 or 0. A total of 1.5 to 2.5 is partial.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error, or a total of 1 or below (e.g., only cost benefits described, with no control trade-off and no conditional fit), or the answer does not address the platform-versus-own-trust comparison.

points.minimum: State that seed capital is fund assets: it is contributed capital that stays invested, is exposed to market risk and may be redeemed. It is not an expense. Keep it separate from one-time launch spending and recurring operating spending, and do not treat the seed amount as a launch budget or a break-even asset level. OPTIONAL subdetails: (a) Investment Company Act §14(a): an ordinary initial public offering requires $100,000 of net worth, subject to the Act's alternative provisions. (b) The point that this $100,000 figure is neither a launch bill nor a commercial break-even level. The §14(a) figure is not independently required, per the round2 resolutions. If an answer cites it, it must be framed as a regulatory net-worth condition and not as a cost.

State that payer allocation is set by contract (the advisory/unitary fee agreement and the platform/trust agreements). Under a unitary fee, the sponsor/adviser pays the covered fund operating expenses out of its fee. Contractually excluded items fall outside the sponsor's obligation: typically brokerage/transaction costs, taxes, interest, extraordinary/litigation expenses and, where applicable, 12b-1 fees. Investors separately bear spreads, trading costs and their own platform charges. The answer must also say who bears organization/launch costs, for example the sponsor, with or without recoupment, as the contract specifies. A generic 'per contract' with no payer assignment is partial. OPTIONAL subdetails: the Lazard filed-response example, in which the manager bears organization costs without recoupment and pays trustees directly under the unitary fee. This example is illustrative and not independently required.

Bundled. Each part is worth half credit.

(3a) Cost categories:
- One-time: at least legal/formation/registration and filing work, plus setup or onboarding with the platform, listing, index and service providers.
- Recurring: at least fund servicing (administration, custody, transfer agency and/or the platform fee), listing, index licensing, and sales/distribution or marketing. Audit, tax, compliance and trustee costs are acceptable additions.
- Costs should be tied to who pays them.

(3b) Break-even:
- Separate annual fixed costs from asset-based variable costs.
- Give break-even AUM ≈ annual fixed costs ÷ (retained fee rate − variable cost rate). An equivalent verbal statement is acceptable.
- State that a break-even level exists only when that per-dollar margin is positive.
- A generic statement that fee revenue (rate × assets) must exceed sponsor costs, or that 'positive margin requires revenue > costs', does NOT satisfy 3b. That earns at most half credit for point 3, provided 3a is met.

OPTIONAL: worked symbolic example; mention of platform minimums or fee floors as fixed costs; the note that the model is simplified, which gives medium confidence.

central_errors: Treating seed capital as an expense, a sunk launch cost or part of the launch budget, or equating the seed amount with break-even assets.
Presenting the §14(a) $100,000 net-worth condition as the cost of launching an ETF, as a quoted launch bill, or as the commercial break-even asset level.

Asserting a specific current vendor quote, or a universal or standard dollar range for launch or annual costs, as fact. This includes promoting an older interview price as the market standard. A clearly hypothetical illustration labelled as such is not an error.

Stating that under a unitary fee the fund or its shareholders pay the covered operating expenses on top of the fee. Also an error: stating that the sponsor bears contractually excluded items such as brokerage, taxes and extraordinary expenses as a matter of course, or that allocation is fixed by law rather than by contract.
Giving a break-even formula that is materially wrong, for example fixed costs × fee rate, or dividing by the gross fee while ignoring variable costs and presenting the result as exact.
Asserting that break-even exists or is reachable when the retained fee rate is less than or equal to the variable cost rate.

scoring_rule.correct: Points 1, 2 and 3 (both 3a and 3b) meet their minimums, and no central error is present. Optional items (§14(a) $100,000, the Lazard example) are not needed for full credit. Minor imprecision does not preclude correct if it does not distort payer allocation, for example listing 'management fee' among recurring costs under a unitary fee. Note any such imprecision.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, but at least one required minimum is unmet or only half met. Score each point at 1, point 3 at 0.5 per sub-part, and point 2 at 0.5 if allocation is called contractual without payer assignment. A total of 1.5–2.5 out of 3 is partial. The canonical case: seed is distinguished, allocation is covered and categories are listed, but break-even is the generic 'revenue must exceed costs' without fixed/variable separation and the positive-margin condition. That answer is partial (2.5/3), consistent with the round2 resolutions.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error is present. Separately, a total below 1.5/3 is wrong, for example when seed versus expenditure is not distinguished and break-even is absent, or when the answer does not address the requested cost/payer structure. Omission alone never triggers a central error. It lowers the score only through unmet minimums.

points.minimum: States that adding a new series to an existing trust by a Rule 485(a) post-effective amendment normally becomes automatically effective 75 days after filing. States that this is a filing-effectiveness clock, not a promised launch date. Optional subdetails: other material 485(a) amendments normally use 60 days; the registrant may designate a later effective date; the SEC may accelerate effectiveness; a citation to Rule 485(a)(1)–(3).

Cites a filed example, such as Simplify's January 30, 2024 485APOS cover, that elects the 75-day route and states that shares cannot be sold before effectiveness. The general principle that shares cannot be sold before effectiveness is acceptable without naming the example.

Explains why 75 days is not an end-to-end launch guarantee. Names at least one source of extra time outside the filing clock: preparatory work, exchange or listing and operational readiness, or separate exemptive relief where needed. Must also distinguish a new trust: it does not use the Rule 485(a) post-effective-amendment route, and the 75-day clock is not the rule for its initial registration. Optional subdetail: a designated later effective date for a new-series amendment may be at most 95 days after filing. A specific commercial launch-time estimate is not required and should not be presented as verified.

central_errors: States that the normal automatic-effectiveness period for adding a new series by 485(a) amendment is 60 days, or another figure other than 75 days.
Presents 75 days, or any filing period, as a guaranteed or binding end-to-end launch or trading deadline.
States that shares may be offered or sold before the amendment becomes effective.
Applies the Rule 485(a) 75-day post-effective-amendment clock to a new trust's initial registration statement, or says the two follow the same process.
States that a new series can be added effective immediately on filing under Rule 485(b) as the normal route.
Presents an unverified universal commercial launch timeline as an established rule.

scoring_rule.correct: Meets the minimum for both required points (1 and 3), including the 75-day figure, the filing-clock-not-launch-guarantee distinction, at least one extra time factor, and the new-trust distinction. Contains no central error. Optional points are not needed for full credit.
scoring_rule.partial: Gives the correct 75-day period with no central error, but only partly covers point 3: for example, it gives the non-guarantee caveat or extra time factors but omits the new-trust distinction, or the reverse. Award half credit for each required point covered only in part. Omissions alone never make an answer wrong.
scoring_rule.wrong: Contains any central error, or fails to identify 75 days as the normal period for a new-series 485(a) amendment, whether by giving no period or a wrong one.

points.minimum: Names the core fund structure and governance plus core service providers. Required: the fund/trust (registered investment company), a board (trustees/directors; officers may be implied), the investment adviser, the distributor/principal underwriter, the custodian, fund administration/fund accounting, the transfer agent and the independent auditor/registered public accounting firm. Equivalent wording is acceptable, for example 'trustees' or 'fund accountant'. A trust is implied when a board of trustees is named. Optional: independent-director composition, sub-adviser, and naming officers separately. Missing one peripheral provider, such as the auditor, makes this point partial. Missing two or more providers, or missing both the board and the trust entirely, makes this point absent.

Covers the ETF-specific market infrastructure. Required: (a) authorized participant agreements and creation/redemption with APs; (b) seed capital or initial seeding/creation; (c) exchange listing; (d) market-making, lead market maker or liquidity provider arrangements; and (e) clearing/settlement (NSCC/DTC or equivalent) with the daily portfolio composition file/basket workflow. Basket or creation-unit processing counts as the PCF workflow. Seed capital and market-making are substantive, not incidental. Omitting either one makes this point at best partial. Omitting both, or omitting the AP arrangements, makes this point absent. Optional: listing-exchange rule detail, IOPV/iNAV dissemination, and the custom-basket policy.

Required: (a) the index licence is needed only for an index-based strategy; and (b) securities lending, with a lending agent, is conditional on running a lending program and is not a universal prerequisite. Also expected: legal counsel (fund and/or independent-trustee counsel) and pricing/valuation support (a pricing vendor or valuation process). Treating the conditional items correctly is the core of this point. If the answer gets the conditionality right but omits counsel and/or pricing, award half credit on this point. Optional: the index calculation agent, the specific lending cash-collateral reinvestment vehicle, and naming the valuation designee under Rule 2a-5.

Explicitly states that roles may be bundled or combined, for example at a service bank, a white-label/series-trust platform or an affiliate, under board oversight. It must also state or clearly convey that the list is a checklist of functions, not a requirement that each role be a separately hired firm. A general bundling statement satisfies this point. Optional: naming specific bundled combinations, such as custody plus administration plus transfer agency at one bank.

Mentions the Rule 38a-1 compliance program and a chief compliance officer, with board approval or oversight (for example approval of policies/CCO, or annual review). Naming the CCO and compliance program without explicit board approval earns half credit on this point. Optional: stating that the CCO or program can be shared or outsourced on a platform. A general bundling statement covers this. Also optional: other required programs, such as the Rule 22e-4 liquidity program, Rule 2a-5 valuation, code of ethics and Rule 18f-4 derivatives.

central_errors: States or clearly implies that every listed role must be a separately hired, unaffiliated firm, or that roles cannot be combined.
States that securities lending or a lending agent is a mandatory prerequisite for every ETF launch.
States that an index licence is required for every ETF, including actively managed ETFs.
States that a '40 Act ETF needs no board, no chief compliance officer or no Rule 38a-1 compliance program, or that those are optional.
States that ETFs do not need authorized participants, or that shares are created and redeemed directly with retail investors.
Describes the product as an unregistered, '33 Act-only commodity pool, or as a UIT-only structure, as the default '40 Act ETF framework, in a way that misframes the governance checklist.

States that the Rule 22e-4 liquidity risk management program applies only if strategy-specific or optional for ETFs. This is a localized error: it caps the grade at partial and does not force wrong unless the answer also makes other central errors.

scoring_rule.correct: All five points are fully met, or at most one point is at half credit for a minor sub-element (for example, counsel/pricing omitted in point 3, or board approval not explicit in point 5) with everything else complete. No central error is present. Seed capital and market-making must both be present for 'correct'. Minor imprecision, such as listing a valuation designee as core, is not penalized.
scoring_rule.partial: There is no forcing central error, and the answer covers the core governance/provider list and at least some ETF infrastructure, but it has substantive gaps. Examples: seed capital or market-making is missing; two or more points are at half credit; one required point is absent; or the answer contains the localized liquidity-program error. Score as half credit overall, or sum the per-point credits (full=1, half=0.5) and map 3.0–4.0 to partial.
scoring_rule.wrong: The answer contains any central error other than the localized liquidity-program error, or it covers fewer than three required points even at half credit (point total below 3.0 with major omissions, such as no ETF-specific infrastructure or no conditional treatment of index/lending). An answer that treats all roles as necessarily separate firms is wrong even if the list is otherwise complete.

points.minimum: Must convey both halves of the allocation: (a) the fund pays the unitary/advisory fee to the platform adviser, and (b) the brand sponsor, under a contract with the adviser, receives the fee remainder after the adviser's share and in exchange assumes the fund's ordinary operating expenses. The sponsor's receipt of the remainder must be stated or clearly implied, not just its expense burden. Saying the adviser 'retains' fee revenue is acceptable if it is immediately qualified by the remainder-for-expenses contract. Optional: label as contractual-partner/expense-partner model; mention of series-trust context.

Must state that the platform adviser remains obligated to the fund to bear the ordinary expenses covered by the unitary fee, even though the sponsor has assumed them by side contract. The sponsor arrangement does not release the adviser; if the sponsor fails to pay, the adviser remains responsible. Optional subdetail, not needed for credit: the unitary-fee obligation is subject to stated exclusions such as brokerage, taxes, interest, acquired-fund fees, and extraordinary or litigation expenses.

Must state or clearly convey that there is no universal or standard percentage split, and must not invent one; any split is negotiated contractually. An answer that is merely silent on the split but invents none earns at most partial on this point. Optional subdetails: the sponsor earns through its contracted share and bears the residual economics, profiting or losing as actual expenses fall below or exceed the remainder; this model differs from appointing the sponsor directly as adviser or sub-adviser.

central_errors: States or implies that the sponsor's assumption of expenses releases or replaces the platform adviser's obligation to the fund, so that the fund must look only to the sponsor.
Presents a specific percentage split (e.g., 50/50, or X bps to the adviser) as the standard or universal allocation.
Describes the model as the sponsor being appointed adviser or sub-adviser, or the fund paying the fee or expenses directly to the sponsor, as the defining mechanism of this arrangement.
States that the fund itself bears ordinary operating expenses outside the unitary fee as a general matter, contradicting the unitary-fee structure.
States that the adviser keeps the entire fee while the sponsor bears expenses with no remainder or compensation, i.e., affirmatively denying that the sponsor receives the fee remainder.

scoring_rule.correct: All three required minima are met and no central error is present. Wording may differ and order is irrelevant. Omission of optional subdetails (exclusions, residual-economics phrasing, contrast with direct sponsor appointment) does not reduce the grade.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error, and at least one required minimum (typically the continuing adviser obligation) is met, but another is missing or muddled. Examples: the sponsor's receipt of the fee remainder is never stated; the sponsor is described as covering only costs 'above the fee's coverage'; receipt and assumption of the remainder are confused; or the answer is silent on the absence of a standard split. Use half credit per bundled point that is partially covered. Unsupported but non-central embellishments, such as the adviser 'must keep the fund solvent', cap the grade at partial.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error is present, or both point 1 and point 2 minima are absent. Example: the answer neither identifies the adviser's continuing obligation nor gives the fee-remainder-for-expenses allocation.

points.minimum: Identifies the brand sponsor/contractual partner (not shareholders, not the fund) as bearing the economic shortfall when assets are too small, under its contractual cost-assumption/expense-sharing arrangement with the platform adviser. Equivalent wording such as 'the sponsor absorbs the loss when unitary-fee revenue falls below fixed costs' suffices. Not required: naming the agreement or describing how fees are split.

States that the platform adviser, a party separate from the brand sponsor/partner, remains contractually obligated to the fund to pay or cover the expenses it promised under the unitary-fee advisory agreement if the partner fails to pay. The answer must name the platform adviser (or the fund's adviser of record, clearly distinguished from the sponsor) as the continuing obligor. Optional subdetails: the adviser's recourse against the partner, or a description of the adviser's counterparty/credit risk.

Bundled context. Half-credit is available for either piece; none is required for a correct grade. (a) Fixed costs mean a small fund's unitary-fee revenue may fail to cover expenses, making it unprofitable for the sponsor. (b) The allocation is contractual and is not a universal obligation for shareholders to reimburse sponsor losses. Optional subdetails: a fixed expense ratio for shareholders, or sponsor incentives to close or merge undersized funds. If (b) is contradicted, see the central errors; that contradiction is not merely an omission of this point.

central_errors: Stating that the fund itself, or its shareholders, bears or owes the unpaid expenses if the sponsor/partner defaults, whether through fund liability, reduced NAV, increased expense ratio, or shareholder reimbursement, as the answer to the second question rather than the platform adviser's continuing obligation.
Stating that shareholders must reimburse sponsor losses or cover the shortfall when assets are too small.

Identifying the sponsor/partner as the party that still owes expenses to the fund after the sponsor's own default (circular), or otherwise naming an obligor other than the platform adviser (e.g., service providers absorb it, the board pays, no one owes).

Treating the sponsor and the platform adviser as one party ('the sponsor (adviser)') in a way that removes the platform adviser's separate backstop obligation. Conflation alone is wrong only when it causes the second answer to miss or misidentify the adviser's backstop. Loose terminology that still clearly assigns the backstop to the platform adviser is not a central error.
Stating that the platform adviser, rather than the sponsor/partner, bears the small-fund economic shortfall in the ordinary course (i.e., reversing the allocation).

scoring_rule.correct: Points 1 and 2 are both satisfied at their minimum, with no central error. Point 3 is not needed. Accept equivalent wording; no citations or set order are required.
scoring_rule.partial: Exactly one of points 1 or 2 is satisfied and the other is omitted or vague, without stating a central error. Example: the answer identifies the sponsor shortfall but says nothing about who owes expenses on default. Also partial: point 2 is gestured at, e.g. 'the adviser remains responsible', but the platform adviser is not clearly distinguished from the sponsor, provided no contrary obligor is named. Point 3 coverage can raise a borderline answer but cannot by itself convert partial to correct.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error is stated, even if point 1 is correct, because the second question's central distinction is contradicted rather than omitted. This includes answers that say the fund remains liable or that shareholders absorb unpaid amounts, with recourse against the sponsor. Also wrong: both points 1 and 2 are omitted or incorrect.

points.minimum: States that appointing a principal underwriter/distributor does not by itself assure a sales force or asset gathering, and frames the appointment as legal/operational distribution (principal underwriter/distributor role for creation-unit and share distribution; not a promise or obligation to raise assets). Optional subdetails: naming the Simplify/Foreside example; noting that Foreside acts as principal underwriter/national distributor; noting the distributor's annual fee and expenses are paid from the adviser's resources; citing the SAI 'Distributor' section. The specific example is not required if the general distinction is stated correctly.

States that salespeople/wholesaling, marketing, and intermediary/platform access (e.g., broker-dealer, RIA, and platform shelf relationships) are separate functions that must be separately allocated or contracted (by the sponsor, adviser, platform, or third parties), and that an ordinary series-trust servicing package cannot be assumed to provide asset gathering. Must reflect that platform packages differ (some may bundle marketing or distribution support, others do not), so packages must be checked case by case rather than assumed to be identical. Optional subdetails: a practical recommendation that sponsors confirm in writing who supplies these functions; examples of what such separate arrangements look like.

central_errors: Asserts that appointing a principal underwriter/distributor on a series-trust platform itself assures or guarantees a sales force, marketing, or asset gathering.
Asserts that the principal underwriter/distributor is contractually obligated to raise assets or deliver AUM targets merely by virtue of the appointment.
Asserts that all series-trust platform packages are identical and uniformly include, or uniformly exclude, sales force, marketing, and intermediary access.
Asserts that every ETF sponsor must legally employ its own in-house sales team (unsupported by the evidence).

Misstates the Simplify example in a way that drives the conclusion, e.g., claiming that Foreside's appointment there includes a commitment to gather assets or that the distributor is paid from fund assets as a sales-force fee, and then uses that claim to conclude asset gathering is assured.

scoring_rule.correct: Both required points meet their minimums: a clear 'no' with the distinction between legal/operational distribution and separately contracted sales, marketing, and intermediary access, plus recognition that platform packages vary. No central error is present. Optional subdetails such as the Foreside/Simplify fee arrangement are not needed for full credit.
scoring_rule.partial: No central error is present, but coverage is incomplete. Award half credit per required point. For example: the answer correctly says the appointment does not assure asset gathering but does not identify sales, marketing, or intermediary access as separately allocated functions. Or it covers point 2 but omits the variability of platform packages, which counts as half of point 2. Or it gives the right conclusion with only a vague distinction. Omissions alone never make an answer wrong.
scoring_rule.wrong: Any central error is stated as a material claim, or the answer's bottom line is that the appointment does assure a sales force or asset gathering. A non-answer, or an answer that fails both required minimums, is also wrong.

points.minimum: States that Rule 6c-11 is available to ETFs organized as registered open-end management investment companies, subject to the rule's conditions, and that UIT ETFs are outside the rule and need separate or existing exemptive relief. Optional subdetails: a list of specific conditions beyond the holdings disclosure in point 3 (basket policies, website disclosures, recordkeeping); the 2019 adoption and the 2019/2020 effective and compliance dates; rescission of older ETF orders.

States that leveraged and inverse ETFs may rely on Rule 6c-11 if they comply with the applicable Rule 18f-4 requirements, so they are not categorically excluded. The answer must link 6c-11 eligibility to 18f-4 compliance. Optional subdetails: the 2020 Rule 18f-4 adoption removed the original 6c-11 exclusion; specifics of 18f-4 (derivatives risk management program, VaR-based limits, limited-derivatives-user exception, leveraged/inverse fund provisions); 18f-4 applies to ETFs generally and not only to leveraged/inverse ETFs.

Bundled point. Minimum for full credit: (a) nontransparent or semi-transparent active ETFs need separate exemptive orders because they do not meet the 6c-11 conditions, at minimum daily public portfolio holdings disclosure; and (b) at least one other structure that needs separate relief, either ETF share classes of multi-class funds or master-feeder ETFs. Covering only one of (a) or (b) earns half credit for this point. Optional subdetails: naming all three structures (nontransparent, master-feeder, share class); any specific recent share-class orders or grandfathering details; an explicit statement that ordinary 6c-11 reliance requires daily website holdings disclosure, beyond its use to explain the nontransparent exclusion.

central_errors: States or implies that leveraged/inverse ETFs are categorically excluded from Rule 6c-11, or must continue to operate only under individual exemptive orders.

States that leveraged/inverse ETFs can rely on Rule 6c-11 without complying with Rule 18f-4, or that 18f-4 compliance is in addition to separate exemptive orders that are still required for leveraged/inverse status.
States that UIT ETFs can rely on Rule 6c-11.

States that nontransparent/semi-transparent active ETFs, ETF share classes, or master-feeder ETFs can rely on Rule 6c-11 alone without separate exemptive relief, or that 6c-11 reliance does not require daily portfolio holdings disclosure.

scoring_rule.correct: All three required points meet their minimums, with equivalent wording accepted, and no central error. Minor incidental inaccuracies outside the central errors may still be graded correct only if they do not affect any eligibility conclusion.
